headline: Lawmakers try to protect children from AI chatbots

sources.title: A reckoning on social media addiction came late for many kids. Will AI safety be different? (AP, via ABC News)
Governor Newsom signs the strongest child safety chatbot and social media laws in the nation (Office of the Governor of California)
Miller-Meeks Introduces Bipartisan Legislation to Protect Children from Human-Like Chatbots (U.S. House of Representatives)

chunks.text: Children today are {{growing up with}} AI chatbots. A [[survey]] by the Pew Research Center found that 64 percent of U.S. teens have used them. The most common uses are to {{look up}} information and to get help with [[schoolwork]]. About 12 percent {{turn to}} chatbots for [[emotional support]] or advice. In early October 2026, a news report asked if governments can act faster on AI than they did on social media.

verbs.correct: To have something in your life as a child
verbs.wrong: To sell something to other kids at school
verbs.why: Many kids grow up with two languages at home. Children on farms grow up with animals all around them. Children today are growing up with AI chatbots.

verbs.correct: To find facts using a book or website
verbs.wrong: To mark mistakes in a student's work
verbs.why: Most people look up words on their phones. Commuters look up bus times before they leave home. The most common uses of chatbots are to look up information and to get help with schoolwork.
When I have money problems, I turn to my brother. Many people turn to their friends after a breakup. About 12 percent of teens in the United States turn to chatbots for emotional support or advice.

chunks.text: Many [[advocates]] say governments {{stepped in}} too late on social media. This summer, Meta reached an $18 billion [[settlement]] with U.S. states and agreed to add stronger [[safeguards]]. Meta did not launch teen accounts on Instagram until 2024. AI companies are now {{rolling out}} similar tools, such as [[age checks]] for [[minors]]. OpenAI introduced teen accounts in August. They [[ban]] romantic chats.

verbs.correct: To act to help or stop a problem
verbs.wrong: To spend money on new schools
verbs.why: Teachers step in when two students start fighting. Some parents step in and pay their adult children's rent. Many advocates say governments stepped in too late on social media.

verbs.correct: To make a new product available
verbs.wrong: To give a product a new name
verbs.why: Banks roll out new apps every few years. Phone companies roll out faster internet one town at a time. AI companies are now rolling out tools such as age checks for minors.

chunks.text: Some experts are {{speaking out}} about the risks. A professor at the University of Chicago says society should not learn about harm only after it happens. A well-known psychologist worries about children's [[emotional attachments]] to chatbots. He also worries when people {{hand over}} their thinking to a bot. Others {{point out}} the [[benefits]]. A tech policy expert at Cornell says AI helps teens with [[tutoring]] and homework. So limits made for social media may not {{carry over}} to AI easily.

verbs.correct: To say publicly what you think
verbs.wrong: To give a talk in another language
verbs.why: Many nurses speak out about their long hours. Some parents speak out at town meetings about school safety. Some experts are speaking out about the risks of AI for children.

verbs.correct: To give a task to someone else
verbs.wrong: To copy a list of answers
verbs.why: Many people hand over their tax forms to an accountant. Busy managers hand over small projects to their assistants. A well-known psychologist worries about people who hand over their thinking to a bot.

verbs.correct: To make people notice a fact
verbs.wrong: To list the costs of a plan
verbs.why: Friends often point out that a store closes early on Sundays. Teachers point out mistakes in essays. Others point out the benefits of AI for teens, such as tutoring.

verbs.correct: To work the same way somewhere new
verbs.wrong: To cost parents a lot of money
verbs.why: Skills from a waiter job often carry over to sales work. Good habits from sports often carry over to school. Limits made for social media may not carry over to AI easily.

chunks.text: Congress has been slow to {{catch up}} with the technology. Some child safety bills on AI have passed Senate subcommittees with support from [[both parties]]. They still face a [[long road]]. On October 1, House members from both parties introduced a bill to stop chatbots from acting human with children. Only parents could {{turn off}} those protections. States are moving faster to {{look out for}} young users. On September 10, California's governor signed laws on [[companion chatbots]], including [[parental controls]] and [[safety audits]].

verbs.correct: To reach the same level as others
verbs.wrong: To take a long summer break
verbs.why: Small stores rarely catch up with big online shops. Students who miss a week of class usually catch up in a few days. Congress has been slow to catch up with AI technology.

verbs.wrong: To pay a fee to a company
verbs.why: Most people turn off their phones during a movie. Many users turn off the location setting on their laptops. Under the new House bill, only parents could turn off the chatbot protections.

verbs.correct: To protect someone and keep them safe
verbs.wrong: To send ads to someone every day
verbs.why: Older kids look out for the younger ones at the park. Good neighbors look out for each other. States are moving faster than Congress to look out for young users.

mainIdea.s: Many children now use AI chatbots, and experts disagree about the risks and benefits. Lawmakers and states are making new rules early, after acting late on social media.
mainIdea.why: Most U.S. teens have used chatbots, and experts are divided. Congress is working on bills, and California has signed new laws on companion chatbots.

mainIdea.s: A national law now stops chatbots from acting human with teens across America. Experts all agree that AI is a bigger danger to children than social media ever was.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the House bill was only introduced on October 1. Experts also disagree, and some point out real benefits like tutoring.

mainIdea.s: A new study found that teens who use AI for homework get better grades in math. Because of this, schools plan to give every student a free tutoring app next year.
mainIdea.why: Lawmakers, states and companies are working to protect children who use AI chatbots. No study on math grades is involved.

tf.s: Many children today are growing up with AI chatbots.
tf.why: A Pew Research Center survey found that most U.S. teens have used AI chatbots.

tf.s: Advocates say governments stepped in early enough on social media.
tf.why: Many advocates say governments stepped in too late on social media, and they want faster action on AI.

tf.s: A tech policy expert at Cornell says AI has no benefits for teens.
tf.why: She points out that teens use AI for tutoring and homework help.

tf.s: AI companies are rolling out safety tools such as age checks for minors.
tf.why: AI companies are now rolling out tools like age checks and teen accounts for young users.

tf.s: Some child safety bills on AI have passed Senate subcommittees.
tf.why: They had support from both parties, but Congress is still trying to catch up and the bills face a long road.

tf.s: The new House bill lets children turn off the protections themselves.
tf.why: Only parents could turn off the protections that stop chatbots from acting human with children.

lines.text: Did you see the news about kids and AI chatbots?
A little. Are a lot of kids really using them?
Yes. About 64 percent of U.S. teens have used one. Kids are {{growing up with}} them now.
What do they use them for? Mostly homework?
Mostly to {{look up}} information and get help with schoolwork. But about 12 percent {{turn to}} them for emotional support.
That part worries me. With social media, we [[learned the hard way]].
That's what a lot of people say. Governments {{stepped in}} really late on social media.
Are the AI companies doing anything this time?
They're {{rolling out}} some safety tools. OpenAI has teen accounts now, with no romantic chats.
Some experts are {{speaking out}}, though. One worries that kids will {{hand over}} their thinking to a bot.
But it also helps with tutoring, right? It sounds like [[a double-edged sword]].
Exactly. One expert {{points out}} that limits for social media might not {{carry over}} to AI.
So what is Congress doing about it?
It's still trying to {{catch up}}. A new House bill would only let parents {{turn off}} the protections.
They're moving faster. California just signed new laws on companion chatbots.
Good. For once, someone is [[ahead of the curve]] when it comes to {{looking out for}} kids.

expressions.def: Used about something that has both good and bad sides

expressions.def: Used to say someone acts before others or before a problem grows
ex: Our school was ahead of the curve on online classes.
